nameStory: The 'kidneyleaf' part of this plant's name comes from its distinctively shaped leaves that look remarkably like tiny kidneys - rounded with a deep notch where the leaf stem attaches. The 'mud plantain' name reflects both where it grows (in muddy, wet places) and its membership in the plantain family, though it's not related to the banana-like plantains we eat!
description: Kidneyleaf mud plantain is a small aquatic flowering plant that hugs the muddy edges of ponds, streams, and wetlands. This low-growing plant rarely gets taller than a few inches and spreads along the ground with its distinctive kidney-shaped leaves. It produces tiny white or pale blue flowers that peek up from the mud during summer. This little wetland gem is extremely rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Unmistakably kidney-shaped leaves that feel smooth and somewhat thick, with a deep rounded notch where the stem connects - just like looking at a tiny human kidney from above

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small white to pale blue flowers with 6 petals that emerge singly from the leaf bases, each about the size of a pencil eraser

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Creeps along muddy surfaces, forming small mats with individual plants staying very low to the ground, rarely exceeding 3-4 inches tall

idTips.label: Habitat Preference
idTips.description: Always found with 'wet feet' - growing directly in mud or shallow water that feels squishy underfoot

habitat: Look for this rare plant along the muddy shores of ponds, slow-moving streams, and seasonal wetlands throughout New England. It prefers spots where the soil stays constantly moist or covered in shallow water, often growing alongside other wetland plants like arrowheads and water lilies. The mud where it grows typically feels soft and squishy, rich with organic matter.

seasonality.spring: New kidney-shaped leaves emerge from the mud as temperatures warm, looking fresh and bright green.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with small white to pale blue blooms appearing among the distinctive leaves. This is the best time for identification.
seasonality.fall: Leaves may persist into early fall but begin to yellow and die back as cooler weather arrives.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely, leaving no visible trace above the mud surface until spring returns.

funFact: This tiny plant is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 4 times by naturalists using modern identification apps - making it rarer to encounter than many animals people spend their whole lives hoping to see!
confusionNotes: The kidney-shaped leaves make this plant nearly impossible to confuse with anything else in New England's wetlands - no other aquatic plant has leaves with such a distinctive kidney shape and deep notch.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'mud plantain,' this plant isn't related to the plantains you might eat (those are bananas) or the common lawn weeds called plantains - it's actually in the water hyacinth family, which explains its love of wet places.
compareHints: Unlike its relative water star-grass which has long, narrow ribbon-like leaves, kidneyleaf mud plantain's leaves are unmistakably broad and kidney-shaped. Water star-grass also tends to grow completely submerged, while kidneyleaf mud plantain prefers to keep its leaves at or just above the mud surface.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water star-grass differs from its relative kidneyleaf mud plantain by being completely aquatic with narrow ribbon leaves, while kidneyleaf mud plantain grows in shallow water or muddy shores with broad, kidney-shaped leaves.
